title: The Basal Ganglia: Reinforcement Learning

html:
The basal ganglia (BG) are the brain’s principal policy optimizer. Each of the brain’s major learning systems occupies a distinct niche in the broader optimization landscape: cortex minimizes precision-weighted prediction error across a deep, recurrent generative model of the world’s causal and statistical structure; hippocampus rapidly encodes one-shot episodic traces that bind context, content, and temporal order into retrievable relational maps; cerebellum performs millisecond-resolution supervised calibration of sensorimotor forward models using climbing-fiber error signals. The basal ganglia solve a complementary problem that none of these systems is designed to handle on its own: selecting, reinforcing, and automating action policies on the basis of delayed, sparse, evaluative feedback. The “actions” subject to this optimization should be understood broadly—not only overt motor outputs such as reaching, saccading, or locomoting, but also covert cognitive and affective operations, including attentional gating, working-memory updating, task-set selection, motivational vigor, and the deployment of abstract decision strategies 1, 2, 3. In active-inference terms, where cortex furnishes much of the state space and predictive structure from which expected free energy is computed, the basal ganglia help convert prior preferences over outcomes into biases over policies, thereby steering both overt and covert action toward preferred states of the world 4, 5. Their niche, then, is not world modeling but world acting: to evaluate candidate actions defined over cortical representations, assign credit for outcomes that may arrive seconds or minutes after the decision that produced them, and progressively compile successful action patterns into efficient, automatized routines. What makes the basal ganglia indispensable is precisely what makes them different from cortex: they do not need to reconstruct the high-dimensional structure of the environment, only to learn which cortical computations to gate, energize, suppress, or crystallize—and to do so under the guidance of a teaching signal (dopaminergic prediction error) whose computational logic is fundamentally evaluative rather than reconstructive. Disrupting posterior dorsomedial striatal activity selectively weakened outcome-dependent, trial-to-trial reinforcement of cued actions. (Figure) 20. Dopamine and striatal projection-neuron activity tracked action outcomes during learning. (Figure). Effort and reward modulate learning across adolescence (Figure) 21. Prediction-error signals reflect reward–effort interactions across adolescence (Figure).

This functional specialization is underwritten by an architecture that differs from cortex in almost every computationally relevant dimension. The cortical sheet is built from recurrent excitatory networks organized into a canonical six-layer columnar motif, in which local pyramidal-cell collaterals sustain persistent activity, lateral inhibition sharpens representations, and laminar segregation supports hierarchical message-passing between levels of abstraction. The striatum—the basal ganglia’s principal input nucleus and the largest structure in the subcortical forebrain—is organized according to very different principles. Its principal projection neurons, the spiny projection neurons (SPNs, also called medium spiny neurons or MSNs), are GABAergic and interact through local inhibitory axon collaterals, rather than the recurrent excitatory circuitry that characterizes cortex, making the striatum poorly suited for the kind of recurrent attractor dynamics thought to support cortical persistent activity and self-supervised error computation 6, 7. Nor does it possess a hierarchical laminar organization: although the striatum contains compartmental (e.g., striosome/matrix) and topographic organization, it lacks the layered vertical axis that gives cortex its capacity for intracolumnar feedforward and feedback signaling 7. Likewise, there is no established analogue of the apical-basal comparison or cortical prediction-error circuitry proposed to support local self-supervised error computation within cortex. Instead, the basal ganglia implement a massively convergent, dopamine-modulated architecture specialized for competitive selection, value-based gating, and reinforcement-driven credit assignment. Cortical afferents converge onto striatal SPNs at enormous ratios—each SPN integrates glutamatergic input from thousands of cortical neurons across multiple cortical areas—and the result of this convergence is funneled through the pallidum and substantia nigra to a small set of thalamic and brainstem targets whose tonic inhibition is selectively released to permit action 8, 9. The striatum is, accordingly, the largest recipient of dopaminergic innervation in the brain, receiving the densest projection from midbrain dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) and ventral tegmental area (VTA)—a fact that reflects the system’s fundamental dependence on dopaminergic teaching signals for synaptic plasticity and credit assignment 10, 11. Where cortex is thought to support local error computation through its recurrent hierarchical circuitry, the basal ganglia instead rely on an extrinsic neuromodulatory teaching signal, and the entire architecture is organized around making that broadcast maximally useful for reinforcement learning and credit assignment. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

Anatomically, the basal ganglia comprise a set of interconnected subcortical nuclei—the striatum (caudate nucleus, putamen, and ventral striatum including the nucleus accumbens), the globus pallidus external and internal segments (GPe and GPi), the subthalamic nucleus (STN), the substantia nigra pars reticulata and pars compacta (SNr and SNc), and the ventral tegmental area (VTA)—whose wiring implements a set of parallel, partially segregated cortico-basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical loops 12, 8. The classical three-channel taxonomy distinguishes motor loops (linking sensorimotor cortex through putamen and ventrolateral thalamus), associative/cognitive loops (linking prefrontal and parietal cortex through caudate and mediodorsal thalamus), and limbic loops (linking orbitofrontal, cingulate, and insular cortex through ventral striatum and ventromedial thalamus), though recent whole-brain mapping has refined this into at least six parallel subnetworks, each transducing a specific cortical information channel through every node of the loop in a bona fide closed circuit, with additional open-loop projections—particularly from ventral striatum through medial SNr to motor thalamus—allowing limbic evaluations to exert a unidirectional influence on motor output 8, 13. It is this loop architecture that constitutes the skeleton on which the reinforcement-learning optimizer is draped: each loop carries a different cortical state representation into the striatum, subjects it to dopamine-modulated competitive selection, and returns the result to the cortical territory from which it originated—thereby allowing a single computational logic (evaluative gating under dopaminergic credit assignment) to be applied in parallel to qualitatively different behavioral domains, from the vigor of a reach to the selection of an attentional set.

Importantly, the basal ganglia resolve their optimization problem through an opponent pathway architecture. The D1-receptor-expressing SPNs of the direct pathway project monosynaptically to GPi/SNr output neurons, whose tonic inhibition of thalamus they suppress, thereby facilitating the selected action; the D2-receptor-expressing SPNs of the indirect pathway project through GPe and STN to the same output neurons, reinforcing tonic inhibition and thereby suppressing competing or contextually inappropriate actions 14, 15. The global loss of the system is resolved through the competitive integration of these two channels: the direct pathway learns the expected value of executing an action, the indirect pathway learns the expected cost of that action or the value of withholding it, and their dynamic balance—modulated in opposite directions by phasic dopamine, which excites D1 SPNs and inhibits D2 SPNs—determines whether a candidate action clears the threshold for release 16, 17. Greater anatomical detail on the intrinsic circuitry, loop organization, and inter-loop interactions of the basal ganglia is provided in “Systems-Level Architecture and Dynamics”; the present section focuses on how this architecture supports learning—what is optimized, what error signal drives the optimization, how that signal modifies the circuit, and what behavioral competences emerge. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

The cellular substrate of this optimization is dominated by the spiny projection neuron. SPNs are a specialized class of GABAergic inhibitory neuron constituting approximately 90–95% of the neuronal population within the striatum, with the remaining 5–10% comprising several classes of interneurons—most prominently the tonically active cholinergic interneurons (CINs), fast-spiking parvalbumin-positive interneurons, and several peptidergic GABAergic interneuron types 10, 18. SPNs exist in two principal phenotypes that map onto the opponent pathway architecture: D1-type SPNs express the D1 family of dopamine receptors (coupled to Gs_s/Golf_{olf} signaling and adenylyl cyclase activation) and project through the direct pathway, while D2-type SPNs express the D2 family of dopamine receptors (coupled to Gi_i/Go_o signaling and adenylyl cyclase inhibition) and project through the indirect pathway. In the dorsal striatum, these two populations are roughly equal in size, largely non-overlapping, and uniformly intermingled, with D1 SPNs comprising approximately 50–52% and D2 SPNs approximately 46–48% of the total SPN population; a small subpopulation (approximately 2% in dorsal striatum, rising to 7–15% in ventral striatum) co-expresses both receptor types, though the functional significance of this co-expressing population remains under active investigation 18, 19. The SPN’s electrophysiology—deeply hyperpolarized resting states enforced by inward-rectifying potassium channels, a requirement for convergent cortical drive to reach spike threshold, and dendritic spine architecture that compartmentalizes individual corticostriatal synapses into semi-independent plasticity units—makes it a neuron exquisitely designed to integrate broad cortical context with a dopaminergic teaching signal at the level of the single synapse. It is this integration, repeated across millions of SPNs organized into opponent D1 and D2 channels within each of the parallel cortico-basal ganglia loops, that constitutes the physical substrate of the reinforcement-learning computation whose loss functions, error signals, plasticity rules, and emergent behavioral competences are detailed in the subsections that follow.
